metadata.title: The Hard Case
metadata.purpose: Answer whether the fix for a struggling student is an easier version of the task -- it isn't. Lands the carry-out that differentiation changes the door in, never the hard case waiting behind it, using the source's own worked case (17 ÷ 5, three tiers, same remainder) as the anchor.

beats.act: hesitant writer cold open / wrong guess
beats.narration_text: Someone assumes the fix for a struggling student is always an easier task. It isn't — that quietly removes the thinking you wanted built. So what actually changes: the task itself, or just the way in?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'so I'll make their task easier?', hesitates on 'easier', corrects to 'different', lands the real question

props.text:
My strugglers cannot
do this. So I will make
their task easier?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('easier' -> 'different') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: Take one problem: seventeen divided by five. Three tiers, one hard case. Below tier: draw seventeen dots, group them by five, circle the two left over. At tier: three, remainder two — a basket analogy, two apples left over. Above tier: same equation, then a proof — why must the remainder always be smaller than the divisor? Three different doors into the same room. Notice what didn't happen: nobody got a simpler problem. The hard case — the remainder — lives in every tier.

shot.new_visual_element: Three tier cards (Below/At/Above) on 17 ÷ 5, all converging on one 'remainder = 2' card

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — three doors, one remainder
production_viz.mechanic: Three stacked cards (Below: dots grouped by 5, 2 circled; At: 3 R2 basket line; Above: proof prompt) each send a line down to one shared card reading REMAINDER = 2, which lights up terracotta. THIS EXACT ANCHOR (the remainder card) RETURNS AT B04.

beats.narration_text: That's the general rule. Differentiation changes the scaffold, the representation, the entry point — never the intellectual demand. Here's the case that breaks the easier-task instinct: give a struggling reader a simpler book, and you've solved today's problem while creating next month's gap — they never practice the hard case at all. Give them the same text with more support instead, and you've given them a real chance to close that gap. Same book. Different scaffold.

shot.new_visual_element: A simpler book (struck, gap grows) beside the same book plus scaffold (gap closes)

production_viz.label: Simpler book, growing gap — same book, closing gap
production_viz.mechanic: Left card: SIMPLER BOOK, a gap bar that grows and turns terracotta over a NEXT MONTH label. Right card: SAME BOOK + SCAFFOLD, the same gap bar shrinking to near zero. A bottom line reads SAME BOOK. DIFFERENT SCAFFOLD.

beats.narration_text: Here's the test for whether you're differentiating or just tracking. Ask one question: does every tier arrive at the same place? Three doors into one room — that's differentiation, and it holds. One entry into three separate ceilings, where the below-tier task caps out lower than the rest — that's tracking, even if it started from a good scaffold. Widening the path keeps everyone in the room. Forking it means some students never reach it at all.

shot.new_visual_element: Two columns: 3 arrows converging on 1 room (differentiation) vs 1 entry forking into 3 capped ceilings (tracking)

production_viz.label: One room, or three ceilings?
production_viz.mechanic: Left column DIFFERENTIATION: three labelled arrows (Below/At/Above) converge into one card, SAME ROOM, lit terracotta. Right column TRACKING: one entry forks into three boxes each capped by a flat lid, one lid drawn visibly lower than the others. Caption under each: 'holds' / 'even from a good scaffold, this is tracking'.

beats.narration_text: Cognitive load theory explains why this matters. Extraneous load is waste — confusing formats, clutter, extra steps — and the scaffold should absorb all of it. Germane load is the actual struggle with the concept, and that is the curriculum itself. Go back to seventeen divided by five: the remainder is germane load. Strip it out to make the task easier, and you haven't simplified anything — you've deleted the lesson.

shot.new_visual_element: Two piles, EXTRANEOUS (absorbed by scaffold) and GERMANE (kept by learner); the REMAINDER = 2 anchor card drops into GERMANE

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — the remainder is germane load
production_viz.mechanic: Two piles side by side: EXTRANEOUS LOAD (clutter icons, an arrow into a card labelled SCAFFOLD ABSORBS) and GERMANE LOAD (an arrow into a card labelled LEARNER KEEPS). THE B01 REMAINDER = 2 CARD RETURNS, identical, and drops into the GERMANE pile. A struck line reads 'strip it out -> not simplified. deleted.'

beats.narration_text: Differentiation changes the door in — never the hard case waiting behind it.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. Take a lesson you already teach. Tell Claude the main concept and the hard case — the exact moment where students get stuck. Ask it to design three tiers: concrete, representational, and abstract, all keeping that same hard case. Then compare the three side by side: does each one actually arrive at the same intellectual demand? Liam, in for Bear.

props.command: Here is my lesson's main concept and the hard case where students get stuck. Design three tiers — concrete, representational, and abstract — that all keep that same hard case. Show me all three side by side so I can compare whether the intellectual demand is the same.
